Part 1 · Fundamentals

Why does zeolite 5A turn air into 96 % oxygen, and which equations describe the bed?

Part 1 · the plan

From one pellet to a two-bed cycle

  1. Equilibrium: extended Langmuir, van’t Hoffhow much N₂ and O₂ the zeolite holds
  2. Selectivity and working capacitywhy swinging the pressure separates
  3. Rate: LDF, breakthrough, MTZwhy part of every bed stays unused

Part 1 · equilibrium

Air is separated by what the zeolite holds back

The guiding question starts at one pellet: what does zeolite 5A do to air?

N₂ held strongly

Its quadrupole meets the cations in the zeolite cages.

O₂ passes

Weaker hold: gas leaving the bed is O₂-rich.

Physical, reversible

Fast, gives off heat; lower pressure releases it.

Argon passes with O₂; textbook and simulator count it with N₂.

Part 1 · equilibrium · one gas

Langmuir: loading rises with pressure, then saturates

$q$
loading: gas held per kg of zeolite
mol/kg
$q_m$
monolayer capacity (all sites filled)
mol/kg
$K$
affinity of the gas for a site
bar⁻¹
$p$
partial pressure of the gas
bar
$$q=\dfrac{q_m K p}{1+Kp}$$

Low $p$: $q\approx q_mKp$ (linear). High $p$: $q\to q_m$ (saturated).

Fitted to pure N₂ and O₂ data on zeolite 5A at 25 °C (Verelst & Baron, 1985).

Part 1 · equilibrium · the mixture

Extended Langmuir: N₂ and O₂ compete for sites

$P$
total pressure in the bed
bar a
$y_i$
mole fraction of gas $i$ (N or O)
–
$$q_i=\dfrac{q_{m,i}K_i\,y_iP}{1+K_N y_NP+K_O y_OP}$$
N₂O₂
$q_{m,i}$ (mol/kg)2.093.26
$K_i$ at 25 °C (bar⁻¹)0.18170.0360

The shared denominator is the competition: more N₂ means less room for O₂.

Part 1 · equilibrium · temperature

A warmer bed holds less: the van’t Hoff term

$T$
bed temperature
K
$b_i$
van’t Hoff constant, $b_i=-\Delta H_i/R$
K
$\Delta H_i,\ R$
heat of adsorption; gas constant 8.314
J/mol, J/(mol·K)
$$K_i(T)=K_{i,25}\,\exp\!\left[b_i\left(\dfrac{1}{T}-\dfrac{1}{298.15}\right)\right]$$
N₂O₂
$b_i$ (K) · $-\Delta H_i$ (kJ/mol)2563 · 21.31476 · 12.3
$K_i$ change per °C at 25 °C−2.8 %−1.6 %

Fits at 0, 25, 45 and 75 °C. N₂ loading from air at 4.5 bar a falls 1.7 % per °C.

Interactive · the model’s isotherm

How much N₂ and O₂ does zeolite 5A hold?

Extended Langmuir + van’t Hoff$q_i=\dfrac{q_{m,i}K_i(T)\,y_iP}{1+\sum_j K_j(T)\,y_jP}$

From air at 4.5 bar a the zeolite holds 0.80 mol N₂ but 0.066 mol O₂ per kg; heating it 10 °C costs a sixth of the N₂.

Part 1 · selectivity · derivation

The separation factor does not depend on pressure

The explorer showed N₂ always ahead of O₂. By how much, and does pressure change it?

$\alpha$
separation factor: loading ratio per unit gas ratio
–
$\alpha\equiv\dfrac{q_N/y_N}{q_O/y_O}$definition: how much more N₂ per unit of N₂ in the gas
$\alpha=\dfrac{q_{m,N}K_N}{q_{m,O}K_O}$insert extended Langmuir: $P$ and the denominator cancel
$\alpha=\dfrac{2.09\times0.1817}{3.26\times0.0360}=3.24$constants at 25 °C

Constant in $P$ and $y$, but temperature-dependent: 4.21 at 5 °C, 2.57 at 45 °C.

Part 1 · working capacity

A bed gives back only what the swing releases

$P_H,\ y_F$
adsorption pressure, N₂ fraction of the feed air
bar a, –
$P_L,\ y_P$
regeneration pressure, N₂ fraction of the purge gas
bar a, –
$\Delta q_N$
N₂ swing (working capacity)
mol/kg
$$\Delta q_N=q_N(P_H,y_F)-q_N(P_L,y_P)$$
$\Delta q_N=0.8021-0.0015=0.8006$air at 4.5 bar a; 96 % O₂ purge at 0.10 bar a
$\dfrac{0.8006\times12\,818}{0.79\times22.31}=582\ \text{s}$bed mass, N₂ feed rate: time to fill the swing

Interactive · swing the pressure

Working capacity: what the pressure swing frees

From the previous slide$\Delta q_N=q_N(P_H,y_F)-q_N(P_L,y_P)$

Purging with product leaves the regenerated end 20 times cleaner than air at 0.10 bar a.

Part 1 · rate

Uptake is fast but not instant: the LDF model

Equilibrium says how much. A moving gas also needs how fast.

$q_i^*$
loading in equilibrium with the local gas
mol/kg
$k_i$
LDF coefficient: N₂ 0.15, O₂ 0.35 (calibrated)
s⁻¹
$\tau_g$
gas time to cross the bed: length × voids ÷ superficial velocity
s
$$\dfrac{dq_i}{dt}=k_i\,(q_i^*-q_i)$$
$1/k_N=6.7\ \text{s}\ \ \text{vs}\ \ \tau_g=\dfrac{5.64\times0.31}{0.0429}=41\ \text{s}$uptake time against gas residence time

The lag spreads the N₂ front into a zone instead of a sharp step.

Part 1 · rate · breakthrough

The front is a zone, and it reaches the top early

$t_b$
breakthrough: outlet N₂ above 5 %
s
$t_s$
stoichiometric time (ideal sharp front)
s
MTZ
mass-transfer zone: partly loaded bed
m
$$t_s=\tfrac12\left(t_{0.05}+t_{0.95}\right)$$

Lab column: 1 m, 4.5 bar a, 0.043 m/s: $t_b$ 75 s, $t_s$ 100 s.

Interactive · the model’s LDF in the lab column

Breakthrough of N₂ from a 1 m zeolite 5A column

LDF uptake$\dfrac{dq_i}{dt}=k_i\,(q_i^*-q_i)$

The model’s $k$ reproduces the lab curve ($t_b$ ≈ 75 s, $t_s$ ≈ 101 s); slower uptake widens the zone and wastes more bed.

Part 1 · bed length · LUB

LUB comes straight from the breakthrough curve

LUB
length of unused bed when $t_b$ is reached
m
$L_{lab}$
length of the lab column
m
$$\text{LUB}=\dfrac{t_s-t_b}{t_s}\,L_{lab}$$
$\text{LUB}=\dfrac{100-75}{100}\times1=0.25\ \text{m}$lab breakthrough at 4.5 bar a, 0.043 m/s

Transfers to the plant only at the same velocity, temperature and pellet size.

Part 1 · the cycle · Skarstrom

Two beds take turns; product purges the other

One bed saturates in minutes. Continuous product needs a second bed and a way to clean it.

$Q,\ Q_D$
volumetric flow in the adsorbing / purged bed
m³/s
$F_D$
purge molar flow
mol/s
$Q_D=Q$rule: same superficial velocity in both beds
$F_D=\dfrac{P_L\,Q_D}{RT}$ideal gas at the regeneration pressure

Purge moles scale with $P_L$: the reason to regenerate under vacuum.

Part 1 · textbook versus simulator · reasons

Four things the steady balance leaves out

Repressurisation

298 of the 389 s go to reaching 4.5 bar a.

O₂-rich zone

2214 mol O₂ held at the end of adsorption; regeneration loses most.

Equalisation

1268 mol cross top to top with 10.5 % N₂.

Heat

Beds swing 22–28.5 °C; $K_N$ falls 2.8 % per °C.

Part 1 · summary

What part 1 settled

  • Extended Langmuir with van’t Hoff gives the loadings; N₂ is held 3.24 times more than O₂.
  • The pressure swing 4.5 → 0.10 bar a with product purge releases 0.80 mol N₂/kg.
  • LDF uptake makes a mass-transfer zone: LUB 0.25 m; LES 5.39 m from the two balances.
  • The real cycle adds EQ and PR; it makes 191.5, not 234 Nm³/h.

The lab velocity fixes the diameterstep 1 of 4

$Q_0,\ Q$
air flow at 0 °C, 1 atm; at 4.5 bar a, 25 °C
Nm³/s, m³/s
$u,\ D$
superficial velocity $Q/A$; bed diameter
m/s, m
Ideal gas$F=\dfrac{PQ}{RT}$
$F_{in}=\dfrac{101\,325\times0.50}{8.314\times273.15}=22.31\ \text{mol/s}$feed at normal conditions

Part 2 · sizing the bed

Two balances give LES and the gas leavingstep 2 of 4

From part 1, for $i$ = N₂ and O₂$(y_{i,in}F_{in}-y_{i,out}F_{out})\,t_b=A\,\text{LES}\,[c_{i,in}\varepsilon+(q_{i,e}-q_{i,0})\rho_b]$
$c_{N,in}=\dfrac{0.79\times4.5\times10^5}{8.314\times298.15}=143.4\ \text{mol/m³}$$c_{O,in}$ = 38.1 the same way
$[\ ]_N=0.31\times143.4+0.8006\times795=681\ \text{mol/m³}$voids + zeolite; O₂: 55.4
$\text{LES}=5.392\ \text{m},\ \ F_{out}=3.398\ \text{mol/s}$solve both balances with $t_b$ = 600 s

The regenerated bed’s void gas is neglected, as in the textbook.

Part 2 · sizing the bed

Add the unused zone, then weigh the bedstep 3 of 4

From part 1$L_B=\text{LES}+\text{LUB}$
$L_B=5.392+0.25=5.64\ \text{m}$LUB from the lab column
$V=A\,L_B=2.858\times5.642=16.12\ \text{m³}$bed volume
$m=\rho_b V=795\times16.12=12\,818\ \text{kg}$zeolite per bed

Installed V-101A/B: Ø 1.91 × 5.64 m, 12.8 t each (simulator 12 847 kg at exactly 1.91 m).

Part 2 · purge and product

Part of the gas leaving cleans the other bedstep 4 of 4

Skarstrom purge rule, part 1$F_D=\dfrac{P_L\,Q_D}{RT},\quad Q_D=Q$
$F_D=\dfrac{0.10\times10^5\times0.1229}{8.314\times298.15}=0.496\ \text{mol/s}$= 40 Nm³/h, FIC-121 set point
$\dfrac{F_D}{F_{out}}=\dfrac{0.496}{3.398}=14.6\ \%$share of the bed product used as purge
$F_P=3.398-0.496=2.90\ \text{mol/s}=234\ \text{Nm³/h}$net O₂ product, 96 %

Recovery $=\dfrac{0.96\times2.90}{0.21\times22.31}=59.4\ \%$ of the O₂ fed.

Interactive · the textbook method with the model’s isotherm

Size a bed for another feed or adsorption time

Diameter follows $\sqrt{\text{feed}}$ and length follows $t_b$: the installed bed fits 1800 Nm³/h for 10 min; 2000 would need 11 % more zeolite.

N₂ left on the zeolite0.0015 mol/kg0.0148 mol/kg

Both cleaned with 96 % O₂ gas; the purge rule makes its moles proportional to $P_L$.

Part 2 · the installed cycle · simulator assumptions, not textbook

Four steps added to the textbook cycle

Equalisation · 30 s

Top to top: saves compressed O₂-rich gas.

Repressurisation · 30 s

Air from V-100 lifts the bed to 1.55 bar a.

Purge · last 180 s

FIC-121 sends 40 Nm³/h of product.

Adsorption · 330–530 s

AIC-124 sets it: 389 s at design.

Part 2 · summary

What part 2 settled

  • The lab velocity set Ø 1.91 m; two balances set LES 5.39 m; LUB added 0.25 m.
  • Vacuum regeneration keeps the purge at 14.6 % of the bed product.
  • K-100 ≈ 114 kW and K-101 ≈ 85 kW make the swing: 1.08 kWh per Nm³ O₂.
  • V-100, V-102 and V-103 absorb the pulses; repressurisation needs a bed hold-down.

“Steady” means every half cycle repeats

Judge over a cycle

Slow trends matter

A step time or end vacuum drifting over hours is the real signal.

Part 3 · the other handles · purge

FIC-121 purges only in steps 2 and 6

The step time is the main handle. Purge, pressure and feed are recipe values.

Path

Product header → FV-121 → top of the bed under vacuum.

Timing

40 Nm³/h for the last 180 s of each adsorption; output held at 0 otherwise.

Effect

Cleaner product end, but every purged mole is lost to V-103.

Interactive · fixed-step runs, 45 min each (Design tab)

Which handle moves purity, and what it costs

Every handle slides the plant along the same purity–production line; the step time reaches furthest at no extra power, so AIC-124 uses it.

Part 3 · the other handles · feed rate

Move the step with the air; AIC-124 trims

Interactive · planned shutdown, 30-min hold, restart (Transition tab)

Where the cycle is held decides the restart

Stopping a machine while KS-140 cycles trips the SIS, so the cycle is held first. But where?

The restart refills V-100 to 4.0 bar a and that air enters the producing bed: hold at a step boundary, not mid-adsorption.

Part 3 · trips

What a trip does to the plant

Cycle held

All XV-111…114 close.

Machines stopped

K-100; also K-101 on I-2 or ESD.

Product diverted

XV-127 vents; FIC-101 MAN 0 %.

Restart

Reset the SIS, then meet the permissives.

ESD on an O₂ fire at V-102: FIC-125 vents it below 1.5 bar a in 16 min (model).

Part 3 · upsets

Three kinds of upset, three time scales

Seconds: a loss

Machine, instrument air or a trip limit: the SIS holds the cycle.

Hours: a drift

Utilities or a filter drift: AIC-124 and FIC-101 compensate.

Cycles: a fault

A valve or transmitter fails: one path goes wrong every cycle.

Recognising each case: the exercises of Part 8.

Part 3 · summary

What part 3 settled

  • Start machines and loops first; KS-140 needs six permissives; sweep V-102.
  • Steady means repeating half cycles; judge purity and production over a full cycle.
  • AIC-124 holds 96 % with the step time; it is slow, so move the step with big changes.
  • Hold the cycle at a step boundary before stopping machines; a trip holds it for you.

Part 4 · summary

What part 4 settled

  • Air is filtered, compressed, cooled and stored in V-100 before the beds.
  • Four XV per bed make the eight steps; a bed produces 389 s of every 898 s.
  • V-102 smooths the O₂ pulses for the customer; V-103 collects the N₂-rich gas.
  • Of 1800 Nm³/h of air, 192 leave as 96 % O₂; recovery 48.6 %.

$R_{O_2}$

The control loops · loop explorer

Nine controllers: what each measures and moves

SP set point · PV measured value · OUT signal to the valve · MAN/AUTO/CAS modes · FC/FO fail closed/open. Eight loops, eight handles, one each.

Which way does the output move?

$$e=\text{PV}-\text{SP}\;\text{(direct)}\qquad e=\text{SP}-\text{PV}\;\text{(reverse)}$$

The model's PID adds $K_c e$ and its integral to OUT; $K_c$ gain, $T_i$ reset time (s).

LoopPV risesOUTso that
TIC-102air warmerupTV-102 passes more chilled water
AIC-124purity higherupa longer step makes more O2

The control loops · fail-safe design

Where each valve goes without air

Each spring is chosen so the failed plant stops making gas and relieves pressure: beds isolated, product vented, receiver blown off, air kept cool.

Two loops that steer the product · step 1 of 2

The O2 buffer: a cascade

PIC-123
outer (master): V-102 pressure → set point of FIC-125; $K_c$ 1.5, $T_i$ 600 s
3.5 bar a
FIC-125
inner (slave): customer flow → FV-125; $K_c$ 0.3, $T_i$ 5 s
≈ 190 Nm³/h

The inner loop answers in seconds (time constant 1.6 s); the buffer drifts over hours.

Two loops that steer the product · step 2 of 2

One hour from design, three ways to run FV-125

A fixed flow above the 191 Nm³/h made empties V-102; the cascade lets the buffer decide the flow. (Model runs, noise off.)

Two loops that steer the product · AIC-124

The purity controller moves a clock, not a valve

KS-140 step time from AIC-124 OUT$t_{AD}=330+2\,\text{OUT}$

Purity high → OUT up → longer adsorption → more O2 per cycle. A new step time waits for the next half cycle.

3600 s

V-102 holds about 49 min of production, so purity answers in tens of minutes: be patient with AIC-124. (Control tab run: step +10 s, AIC-124 in MAN.)

Two beds, half a cycle apart

AD adsorption · PG evacuation with O2 purge · EQ equalisation · BD blowdown · EV evacuation · PR feed repressurisation. Durations at design.

XV-111 feed in · XV-112 to vacuum · XV-113 product out · XV-114 top-to-top EQ and purge.

    Part 5 · summary

    What part 5 settled

    • A tag reads as measured variable + function; XI tags are half-cycle calculations.
    • Eight loops use eight handles; every valve fails to the side that stops gas and relieves pressure.
    • PIC-123 lets V-102 choose the customer flow; AIC-124 trims the step time, slowly.
    • KS-140 runs eight steps; four fail-closed valves per bed define each one.
    • Alarm, SIS trip and relief valve sit in layers; six permissives guard the start.

    Around the beds, in the order the gas meets them

    1. Air sideF-100 filter, K-100 screw compressor on a VSD, E-100 aftercooler

    Around the beds · map

    Eleven units serve two beds

    Parts 1–4 were about the beds. Every other unit exists to feed them, empty them or smooth what they make.

    Click a unit

    Numbers are the model's design values.

    Air side, vacuum side, product side: each side has one machine or one buffer that sets its limit.

    Air side · step 1 of 4

    F-100: a pressure drop that grows with flow

    Clean filter, as in the model$\Delta p=\Delta p_0\left(F/F_0\right)^2$

    $\Delta p_0$ = 8 mbar at $F_0$ = 1800 Nm³/h; PDI-100 alarms at 40 mbar. Change the element on the alarm, not on the calendar.

    Air side · step 2 of 4

    K-100: an oil-free screw on a variable-speed drive

    $F_c$
    air delivered
    mol/s
    $F_{max}$
    delivery at 100 % speed, low discharge pressure
    28 mol/s
    $N$
    speed, SI-100
    %
    $p_{100}$
    V-100 (discharge) pressure
    bar a
    $W$
    motor power, JI-100
    kW
    $$F_c=F_{max}\,\frac{N}{100}\left(1.08-0.08\,\frac{p_{100}}{5.2}\right)\qquad W=\frac{F_c R T\ln(p_{100}/p_{suc})}{0.72}+12\,\frac{N}{80}$$

    Isothermal power over an assumed 72 % efficiency, plus a 12 kW speed-loss term (model).

    Air side · step 3 of 4

    Speed sets the flow; pressure trims it

    From the previous slide$F_c=F_{max}\tfrac{N}{100}\left(1.08-0.08\tfrac{p_{100}}{5.2}\right)$

    Over one cycle V-100 swings 2.7–5.5 bar a; at fixed speed the air would swing with it, so FIC-101 keeps moving the VSD.

    Air side · step 4 of 4

    E-100: cool air is worth capacity

    Aftercooler, as in the model$T_{air}=T_{hot}-\varepsilon\,(T_{hot}-T_{chw})$
    Effectiveness$\varepsilon=1-e^{-1.2\sqrt{x/100}}$

    $T_{hot}$ = 45 °C from K-100. Warmer air, less N2 held: the isotherm's K for N2 falls about 2.8 % per °C.

    Receiver and drain · step 1 of 2

    V-100 turns pulses into a steady compressor load

    Ideal-gas buffer$\dfrac{dp}{dt}=\dfrac{RT}{V}\,(F_{in}-F_{out})$

    The swing scales as $1/V$ (first estimate, same flows). At 20 m³ it stays below the 6.2 bar a blow-off.

    Receiver and drain · step 2 of 2

    Compressing and cooling air makes water

    Trap DT-104 drains V-100; HV-104 bypasses it. Liquid water reaching a bed poisons the zeolite from the bottom, for good.

    Vacuum side · step 1 of 3

    K-101: a liquid-ring pump has a floor

    $F_p$
    gas pumped
    mol/s
    $S_0$
    displacement (model constant)
    0.9 m³/s
    $p_v$
    suction pressure, vacuum header PI-131
    bar a
    $T_{sw}$
    seal-water temperature, TI-132
    °C
    $p_{lim}$
    vacuum floor: seal water boils into the ring
    bar a
    $$F_p=\frac{S_0\,(p_v-p_{lim})\times10^5}{R\,T_{sw}}\qquad p_{lim}=p_{sat}(T_{sw})+0.012$$

    0.012 bar is the model's leakage allowance; $p_{sat}$ from the Antoine equation of water.

    Vacuum side · step 2 of 3

    Pumping speed falls to zero at the floor

    From the previous slide$F_p=S_0(p_v-p_{lim})10^5/(RT_{sw})$

    The deeper the vacuum, the less gas each turn moves and the more each mole costs: the last 0.1 bar is the slowest and the dearest.

    Vacuum side · step 3 of 3

    Blowdown gas skips the pump

    V-104 separates the seal water from the gas before V-103.

    While the header is above V-103 the check valve CV-130 opens: blowdown flows free, K-101 only pulls below 1.25 bar a.

    Product and by-product · step 1 of 3

    V-102: minutes of product in reserve

    Stored gas in a 50 m³ buffer at 25 °C$\dfrac{dN}{dp}=\dfrac{V}{RT}\;\Rightarrow\;45.2\ \text{Nm}^3\text{ per bar}$

    The buffer buys time, not product: a draw above what the beds make always ends at the low alarm.

    Product and by-product · step 2 of 3

    Three valves decide where the O2 goes

    ValveJobFails
    FV-125meters the product, FIC-125shut
    XV-126opens to the customer header, 2.5 bar ashut
    XV-127opens to the off-spec ventopen

    Route to the customer at AT-124 ≥ 93 %; I-6 vents below 90 % for 10 s. Below 95 % the customer pays half price.

    Product and by-product · step 3 of 3

    V-103 and the three buffers over one cycle

    V-103 gas is about 12 % O2: an asphyxiation hazard at the HV-136 vent and wherever it leaks.

    The energy bill

    Two machines, one number

    XI-142, from part 5$e=\dfrac{W_{K100}+W_{K101}}{F_{O_2}\,y_{O_2}}$

    Both machines run the whole cycle; power changes little, so every extra Nm³ of O2 lowers the kWh per Nm³.

    Part 7 · summary

    What part 7 settled

    • F-100, K-100 and E-100 deliver 1800 Nm³/h of clean air at 25 °C; FIC-101 rides the receiver swing with the VSD.
    • V-100 smooths the bed pulses; DT-104 keeps water out of the zeolite.
    • K-101 has a vacuum floor set by its seal water; CV-130 takes the blowdown past it.
    • V-102 and V-103 buy minutes, not product; three valves route the O2.
    • About 199 kW for 183 Nm³/h of pure O2: 1.08 kWh/Nm³.

      Procedure P1 of 6 · steps 1–4

      Cold start-up (graded)

      P1limit 5 hgraded out of 10

      Bring the plant from cold to 96 % O2 at the customer, in order, safely, in time.

      Both beds full of air at 1 atm, machines stopped, cycle stopped, V-102 full of air. Start the machines and the cycle, clean up the O2 buffer and deliver 96 % O2.

      1. Open the K-101 seal water and start K-101
      2. Chilled water to E-100 open, TIC-102 in AUTO at 25 ±2 °C (any time)
      3. Start K-100 (FIC-101 in MAN) and bring V-100 to 4.0 bar a or more
      4. PIC-122 in AUTO at 4.5 bar a and FIC-121 in AUTO at 40 Nm³/h (any time)

      Procedure P1 of 6 · steps 5–8

      Cold start-up (graded)

      P1limit 5 hgraded out of 10
      1. PIC-133 in AUTO at 1.25 bar a (any time)
      2. Start the KS-140 cycle (product still to the vent)
      3. FIC-101 in AUTO at 1800 ±20 Nm³/h
      4. Sweep the air out of V-102: FIC-125 in MAN at 80 % or more (V-102 stays low, product to the vent) (any time)

      Procedure P1 of 6 · steps 9–13

      Cold start-up (graded)

      P1limit 5 hgraded out of 10
      1. O2 purity AT-124 at 95.5 % or more
      2. PIC-123 in AUTO at 3.5 bar a with FIC-125 in CASCADE (build up the buffer)
      3. Product routed to the customer (XV-126 open, XV-127 shut)
      4. AIC-124 in AUTO with its set point at 96 %
      5. Hold 10 minutes in band (AT-124 ≥ 95.5 %, O2 made ≥ 170 Nm³/h, product to the customer)

      Procedure P2 of 6 · steps 1–4

      Restart after a vacuum-pump trip (graded)

      P2limit 2 hgraded out of 10

      Restart a held plant after a machine trip and line it out.

      K-101 tripped 30 minutes ago (I-2); the cycle is held, both machines are stopped and the product diverted. The pump is repaired. Restart and line out.

      1. Reset the SIS
      2. Seal water open and K-101 running
      3. K-100 running and V-100 at 4.0 bar a or more
      4. PIC-122, FIC-121 and PIC-133 in AUTO (any time)

      Procedure P2 of 6 · steps 5–9

      Restart after a vacuum-pump trip (graded)

      P2limit 2 hgraded out of 10
      1. Cycle running (start / resume KS-140)
      2. FIC-101 in AUTO at 1800 ±20 Nm³/h
      3. AT-124 ≥ 95.5 % and product routed to the customer
      4. FIC-125 in CASCADE and AIC-124 in AUTO at 96 %
      5. Hold 10 minutes in band

      Procedure P3 of 6

      Planned shutdown (graded)

      P3limit 1 hgraded out of 10

      Stop the plant so that it can restart cleanly.

      Planned stop from design: stop deliveries, hold the cycle at a step boundary, stop the machines.

      1. Tell the O2 customer and the N2 users
      2. Stop deliveries: FIC-125 in MAN at 0 % (V-102 stays full of product)
      3. Hold the cycle at a step boundary: in step 4 or 8 (BD/PR) or in the first minute of step 1 or 5, so the restart is clean
      4. Stop K-100
      5. Stop K-101 and close its seal water
      6. FIC-101, PIC-122, FIC-121 and AIC-124 in MAN

      Procedure P4 of 6

      Emergency shutdown (graded)

      P4limit 30 mingraded out of 10

      Act on an emergency order at once and make the O2 buffer safe.

      An emergency arrives shortly after loading.

      1. Push the emergency shutdown (I-5)
      2. Product diverted and FIC-125 in MAN (any time)
      3. Vent V-102 through FV-125: FIC-125 output 50 % or more
      4. V-102 below 1.5 bar a

      Procedure P5 of 6

      Low purity at the customer: recover (graded)

      P5limit 1 h 30 mingraded out of 10

      Recover a purity complaint as a procedure: verify, act, confirm, report.

      The situation of TE-1 with the procedure tracker on.

      1. Four steps; they appear on the procedure tracker when you load this procedure.

      Procedure P6 of 6

      Optimisation, 45 min (graded)

      P6limit 45 minlive: graded at the end

      Make more O2 at spec from the same plant by moving the feed, the step time and the purge.

      Make at least 200 Nm³/h of O2 at 95.5 % or better from the same plant by moving the feed air, the adsorption step time and the purge.

      1. O2 production XI-144 ≥ 200 Nm³/h at the end
      2. O2 made in the last half cycle XI-143 ≥ 95.5 %
      3. O2 purity AT-124 ≥ 95.5 % and product to the customer
      4. No alarm active and none unacknowledged

      Troubleshooting cases · the method

      Six stages for every case

      Every case below is worked on the Workbook's six-stage sheet; the stage you skip is where cases go wrong.

      1 Engage

      Who is at risk? Run, vent, hold or stop.

      2 Define

      What, where, when, how much.

      3 Explore

      Isotherm, balances, instruments.

      4 Plan

      Three hypotheses, each with a test.

      5 Do it

      Predict, test, fix the root cause.

      6 Look back

      Stop it happening again.

      Troubleshooting case · TE-1

      TE-1 · Customer complains of low purity

      TE-1starts with 1 h of historysix-stage worksheet

      Resolve a purity complaint: protect the customer first, then find the root cause with evidence.

      The customer says their own analyzer reads 91-93 % O2 in our product. Our AT-124 reads 96.4 % and AIC-124 is in AUTO. Production is higher than usual (about 235 Nm³/h) and the adsorption step is longer than it used to be.

      Troubleshooting case · TE-2

      TE-2 · Step time keeps getting shorter

      TE-2starts with 1 h 30 min of historysix-stage worksheet

      Explain a slow, steady loss of separation and stop it before the product goes off-spec.

      Over the last hour and a half AIC-124 has shortened the adsorption step from about 389 to 371 s and it is still falling. AT-124 is 94.6 % and slowly dropping. Air flow and pressures look normal.

      Troubleshooting case · TE-3

      TE-3 · Vacuum not as deep as it used to be

      TE-3starts with 1 h of historysix-stage worksheet

      Find why regeneration has weakened and restore the end vacuum.

      The end-of-evacuation pressure has crept up over the last hour; XI-146 now reads 0.22 bar a (normal 0.10). Purity is about 94 % and the step is shorter than normal.

      Troubleshooting case · TE-4

      TE-4 · Vacuum not as deep, pump sounds normal

      TE-4starts with 1 h of historysix-stage worksheet

      Diagnose a poorer end vacuum from console and field evidence, and restore it.

      The end-of-evacuation pressure has crept up to 0.19 bar a over the last hour. The K-101 motor current and noise are normal. Purity 94.9 %.

      Troubleshooting case · TE-5

      TE-5 · Every other half cycle is poor

      TE-5starts with 30 min of historysix-stage worksheet

      Localise an uneven cycle with the half-cycle report, then confirm in the field.

      Production is down to about 150 Nm³/h. The product flow pulses are uneven: one half cycle makes much more than the other. AT-124 reads 96.2 %.

      Troubleshooting case · TE-6

      TE-6 · Half cycles with bed A producing are poorer

      TE-6starts with 1 h of historysix-stage worksheet

      Find what differs between the two beds and fix it without losing the customer.

      The half-cycle log shows that the half cycles in which bed A produces are about 2 % O2 poorer than those of bed B. Production is down to about 175 Nm³/h. No valve alarms.

      Troubleshooting case · TE-7

      TE-7 · Production down, purity fine

      TE-7starts with 40 min of historysix-stage worksheet

      Find a small loss of production and recovery while every loop sits at its set point.

      Production has dropped from 192 to about 184 Nm³/h and recovery from 48.7 to 47 %. Purity is on target, FIC-121 shows 40 Nm³/h at its set point, and the end-of-evacuation pressure is a little higher (0.112 bar a).

      Troubleshooting case · TE-8

      TE-8 · Purity above target, production well down

      TE-8starts with 45 min of historysix-stage worksheet

      Restore production when purity is high and the customer is short, keeping the spec.

      The day shift reports O2 at 96.7 % and rising, but production is only about 127 Nm³/h and the customer is short. The only alarms are low customer flow, low O2 recovery and low N2-rich purity.

      Troubleshooting case · TE-9

      TE-9 · No O2 production at all

      TE-9starts with 20 min of historysix-stage worksheet

      Respond to a total loss of production: protect the buffer and the customer, then find the cause.

      Product flow has stopped: XI-144 reads 0 and V-102 has fallen to 2.6 bar a. AT-124 is frozen at 96 %. The cycle is running and both beds swing between vacuum and pressure.

      Troubleshooting case · TE-10

      TE-10 · Feed air cannot reach its set point

      TE-10starts with 1 h of historysix-stage worksheet

      Find why the feed loop has run out of handle and restore the air rate.

      FIC-101 is in AUTO at 1800 Nm³/h but reads 1769 and its output is at 100 %. Production is about 174 Nm³/h.

      Troubleshooting case · TE-11

      TE-11 · Bed B pressure trend looks strange

      TE-11starts with 20 min of historysix-stage worksheet

      Decide what a strange trend means and keep the plant safe while you find out.

      The bed B pressure PI-115B shows a flat line on the trend although the cycle is stepping normally. Production and purity are normal.

      Troubleshooting case · TE-12

      TE-12 · Customer gets less O2 than the plant makes

      TE-12starts with 40 min of historysix-stage worksheet

      Resolve a delivery shortfall with the six-stage method and evidence.

      The customer receives about 127 Nm³/h while the plant display says 191 Nm³/h O2 at 96 % is made. V-102 is a little low (3.3 bar a).

      Short drills · step 1 of 3

      Trend matching

      Recognise an event from the shape of six pens over 15 minutes from design.

      Four unlabelled trend sets are drawn from these events; name each and justify it from the pens.

      1. Feed air raised 10 %
      2. Vacuum pump K-101 trips
      3. Adsorption step lengthened by hand (AIC-124 MAN, +40 s)
      4. Chilled water to E-100 lost
      5. XV-112B fails to open
      6. Purge flow doubled (FIC-121 80 Nm³/h)

      Short drills · step 2 of 3

      What-if predictions

      Predict ↑, ↓ or = for eight variables 30 minutes after an event, then explain every miss.

      Six events

      1. Feed air +10 % (FIC-101 SP 1980)
      2. Purge doubled (FIC-121 SP 80)
      3. Adsorption pressure 4.0 bar a (PIC-122 SP)
      4. Adsorption step +40 s (AIC-124 MAN)
      5. Chilled water to E-100 lost
      6. Vacuum pump capacity −50 %

      Eight variables

      • AT-124 O2 purity (buffer)
      • XI-144 O2 production
      • XI-141 O2 recovery
      • XI-146 end-of-evacuation pressure
      • XI-145 adsorption step time
      • XI-142 specific power
      • AT-135 N2-rich purity
      • TI-117A bed A middle temperature

      Short drills · step 3 of 3

      Scrambles and the DCS reading sheet

      Order the steps of a procedure from memory; read values and alarm limits off the console.

      Scrambles: Cold start-up (9 steps); Emergency shutdown (ESD) (6 steps); Restart after a vacuum-pump trip (8 steps).

      Reading sheet, 18 tags: FIC-101, TIC-102, AIC-124, PIC-123, FIC-125, PIC-133, AI-135, XI-141, XI-142, XI-143, XI-144, XI-145, XI-146, TI-116A, TI-118A, TI-132, PDI-100, SI-100.

      Part 8 · summary

      What part 8 settled

      • Seven kinds of exercise: three run the plant, four read it.
      • The score starts at 100; procedures are graded out of 10 for safety, order, time and communication.
      • Six procedures, 20 training exercises and 12 troubleshooting cases, each with its objective.
      • Troubleshooting follows six stages: engage, define, explore, plan, do it, look back.

      The whole deck

      Key Takeaways

      1

      Judge the plant over a full cycle: read the XI tags, not one snapshot.

      2

      Keep the N2 front below the top of the bed; feed, step, vacuum, temperature and purge all move it.

      3

      Let AIC-124 trim slowly and PIC-123 set the customer flow; move one handle at a time.

      4

      Protect people and the customer first: alarm, then SIS, then relief valve.

      5

      Troubleshoot in six stages, with evidence for every claim.
